According to tradition, the city was established by the twin brothers Romulus and Remus, descendants of the Trojan hero Aeneas and the god Mars, following the fall of Troy. After a dispute over the site of their new settlement, Romulus slew his brother and founded the city, naming it after himself. In this earliest phase, known as the Kingdom of Rome, the city was ruled by seven kings, initially of Sabine origin and later of Etruscan influence, most notably Tarquinius Priscus and his son Tarquinius Superbus. The political structure was strictly monarchic and patriarchal, with the King (Rex) holding supreme authority over military, religious, and judicial matters, advised by the Senate, a council of patrician elders, and the Comitia Curiata, an assembly organized by curiae, or patrician families. The origins of the Roman Republic are shrouded in a blend of historical evidence and enduring mythology, traditionally dated to 509 BCE following the expulsion of Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, the last Etruscan king of Rome. The immediate catalyst for this political upheaval was the violation of the sacred boundaries of Vestal Virginess by the king’s son, Sextus, and the general oppression of the plebeians, who were heavily taxed and denied political voice. In the vacuum left by the monarchy, the Roman elite, known as the *patricii*, established a republican system designed to prevent the return of autocratic rule. They created the office of the consul, two annually elected magistrates with supreme executive power but limited to a one-year term and constrained by mutual veto, thereby ensuring that no single individual could accumulate unchecked authority. This foundational moment marked a decisive shift from personal rule to rule by law and the collective wisdom of the Senate, although in practice, political power remained tightly concentrated in the hands of a few wealthy aristocratic families who dominated the new political institutions.

When launching kernels eagerly, the CPU must execute a series of API calls (such as `cudaLaunchKernel`) for each kernel in the sequence, involving memory allocation, parameter packing, and command queue submission. This per-kernel overhead can become significant for graphs with many small kernels or when the GPU is fast enough to finish executing them quickly, creating a bottleneck where the GPU idles waiting for the CPU to issue the next command. By contrast, a CUDA graph captures the entire dependency structure of these kernels into a single, pre-compiled execution plan. During replay, the CPU issues only a single command to the GPU to execute the entire graph, shifting the scheduling logic to the GPU’s own hardware. This allows for deep pipelining and concurrent execution of independent branches within the graph with minimal CPU intervention.

The primary reason a CUDA graph replay can be significantly faster than launching the same kernels eagerly is the reduction of CPU overhead and driver API call latency. In eager execution, every kernel launch requires a CPU-side call to the CUDA runtime (e.g., `cudaLaunchKernel`), which involves validation, parameter copying, and submission to the GPU command stream. When launching many small kernels, the CPU can become a bottleneck because it cannot keep up with the pace of the GPU, leading to gaps in GPU utilization. A CUDA graph captures this sequence of kernels once and compiles them into a single, optimized execution plan. Replaying this graph requires only a single, lightweight API call from the CPU (`cudaGraphLaunch`), allowing the CPU to get out of the way while the GPU executes the entire batch of operations with minimal stalls.

Furthermore, CUDA graphs enable deeper hardware-level optimizations that are not possible with individual eager launches. The CUDA driver can perform global optimization across the captured dependencies, such as merging small operations, pre-allocating memory, and scheduling kernels in a way that maximizes parallelism and minimizes synchronization overhead.
